name: Roussanne

lines.s10: Roussanne is the scented white of the Rhône: ripe pear, honeysuckle and chamomile tea on a rich, silky body that stays fresh.
lines.s20: Roussanne is Marsanne's partner in the white wines of the Rhône, and the finer scented of the two. It smells of ripe pear, honeysuckle and chamomile tea, and it is full and silky with enough acidity to age.
lines.s45: Roussanne tests the patience of growers in the white Rhône, and repays it. It grows from Hermitage down to Châteauneuf-du-Pape, and it climbs into Savoie under the name Bergeron. It smells of ripe pear, honeysuckle and chamomile tea. It is full and silky, with more freshness than its partner, Marsanne. The Rhône tends to blend it and raise it in barrel, while California's Central Coast usually makes it riper and more honeyed. It flatters crab, roast veal or a mushroom risotto. A good many California vines sold as Roussanne in the 1990s turned out to be Viognier.
lines.sale: Roussanne is hard to grow, and one glass shows why growers bother: honeyed pear and honeysuckle, held up by a fresh finish. Try it with the crab or the roast veal.

glass.lead: Ripe pear, honeysuckle and chamomile tea with a touch of honey, on a full, silky body kept fresh by its acidity.

ladder.where: Chignin-Bergeron in Savoie, on sunny limestone scree
Châteauneuf-du-Pape, the Languedoc, California's Central Coast

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium, fresher than Marsanne's, alcohol medium to high, body full, with a silky, slightly oily texture.

home.home: The Rhône, where it is mostly blended: with Marsanne in white Hermitage and Saint-Joseph, with Grenache Blanc and Clairette in white Châteauneuf-du-Pape, often in barrel. It brings ripe pear, honeysuckle and chamomile tea and a fresh finish. Savoie bottles it alone as Chignin-Bergeron, rich yet fresh, with apricot and honey.
home.abroad: California's Central Coast, Washington and the Swartland grow it, mostly for Rhône style blends with Marsanne, Viognier and Grenache Blanc. Some is bottled alone, typically riper and broader, with baked pear, acacia honey and roasted almond.

service.temp: 50 to 55 degrees Fahrenheit, 10 to 13 degrees Celsius: too cold and the scent and the texture hide.
service.glass: A white wine glass with a generous bowl; a Burgundy bowl for a rich, mature wine.
service.decant: Rarely. A young, closed white Rhône can open with a short decant; taste a sample first.
service.age: Most within three to six years; white Hermitage and serious Châteauneuf whites keep ten years or more.

with.dish: Crab cakes or crab in butter
with.why: silky weight for sweet, rich crabmeat

with.dish: Roast veal or pork with cream
with.why: body to match, freshness to cut the cream
honey and roasted almond suit the mushrooms
the tea and honeysuckle scent echo the herbs

labels.means: Roussanne's name in Savoie, and the cru made from it alone, on limestone scree.
The southern Rhône white: Roussanne with Grenache Blanc, Clairette and Bourboulenc. Marsanne is not permitted there.
Roussanne with Marsanne, Viognier or Grenache Blanc, wherever in the world it is made.

guest.q: I always see Roussanne next to Marsanne. Are they alike?
guest.a: They are partners. Marsanne gives weight and a waxy feel, and Roussanne brings the perfume, the freshness and much of the capacity to age. Roussanne is the harder of the two to grow.

guest.q: What does it taste like next to a Chardonnay?
guest.a: As full, but more scented: ripe pear, honeysuckle and a note like chamomile tea, with a silky, slightly oily feel and usually less obvious oak.

guest.q: What is Bergeron on this Savoie list?
guest.a: It is Roussanne. Savoie calls the grape Bergeron, and Chignin-Bergeron is its own cru there: rich yet fresh, with apricot and honey.

compare.tell: Marsanne is broader, waxier and nuttier, with lower acidity; Roussanne is the more scented, with chamomile tea and a fresher finish.
Viognier is headier and louder, all apricot and honeysuckle on low acidity; Roussanne is subtler, with pear, chamomile tea and more freshness.
Grenache Blanc is plainer in scent, with green apple, fennel and a warm finish; Roussanne is more perfumed and more honeyed.

profile.st: Deep straw to gold · Body full · Acid medium · Alcohol medium to high · Dry · Silky, slightly oily texture
profile.fruit: Ripe pear, apricot, white peach; baked pear and yellow apple from warm sites
profile.other: Honeysuckle, iris, hawthorn blossom and chamomile tea; acacia honey and beeswax; roasted almond and hazelnut with age
profile.tell: A full, silky white of pear, honeysuckle and chamomile tea, with a fresher finish than its weight suggests
profile.regions: Hermitage, Crozes-Hermitage, Saint-Joseph and Saint-Péray with Marsanne; Châteauneuf-du-Pape blanc; Savoie as Bergeron (Chignin-Bergeron); California's Central Coast; Washington; the Swartland
profile.confuse: Marsanne is waxier, nuttier and lower in acid; Viognier is louder, with apricot and less acid; oaked Chardonnay shows butter and toast and no tea note

cards.front: Roussanne: what is it called in Savoie, and which cru is its own?
cards.back: Bergeron. Chignin-Bergeron is made from Roussanne alone, grown on limestone scree: rich yet fresh, with apricot and honey.

cards.front: Roussanne abroad: where is it grown, and how is it mostly used?
cards.back: California's Central Coast, Washington and the Swartland, mostly in Rhône style blends with Marsanne, Viognier and Grenache Blanc. Some is bottled alone, riper and more honeyed than at home.

cards.front: Which white grapes may join Roussanne in a Châteauneuf-du-Pape blanc?
cards.back: Grenache Blanc, Clairette, Bourboulenc, Picpoul and Picardan. Marsanne and Viognier are not among the appellation's permitted grapes.

questions.q: A blind white from Saint-Joseph is full and silky, with ripe pear, honeysuckle and chamomile tea and a fresh finish. Which grape most likely brings the scent?
questions.exp: Pear, honeysuckle and chamomile tea with a fresh finish mark Roussanne, the scented half of the northern Rhône's white blend. Marsanne, its partner, is broader, waxier and nuttier, and Viognier would smell loudly of apricot.

questions.q: A guest in a Savoie restaurant orders a Chignin-Bergeron and asks which grape it is made from. What do you tell him?
questions.exp: Bergeron is Savoie's name for Roussanne, and Chignin-Bergeron is made from it alone. Plain Chignin is chiefly Jacquère, and Altesse is the grape of Roussette de Savoie.

questions.q: A guest who knows the white grapes of the northern Rhône asks what the Châteauneuf-du-Pape blanc on the list can hold. Which pair may that appellation use?
questions.exp: Roussanne and Grenache Blanc are both on the list Châteauneuf-du-Pape permits, with Clairette and Bourboulenc. Marsanne and Viognier are not, though both make white wine in the northern Rhône.

report: Mode contrast, as the plan fixes it: the Rhône and Savoie against the varietal bottles of California's Central Coast, with Washington and the Swartland beside them. The New World style is thinner on the ground than for most side by side grapes; a reviewer may judge it a home grape.

A Codex record believed wrong: INTRO_GRAPES gives Roussanne's wines as Hermitage, Châteauneuf-du-Pape blanc (with Marsanne). Marsanne is not among the grapes the Châteauneuf-du-Pape rule permits; the appellation's own cahier des charges lists bourboulenc, clairette, grenache blanc, picardan, piquepoul blanc and roussanne for white. The entry says so in a label row, a card and a question.

The Codex's Régionale bank says Roussanne ripens late; Inter Rhône's grape page, as the search returned it, calls it early to mid ripening. The entry states neither and says only that it is the harder of the two to grow.
The Régionale row says herbal tea; the entry names it chamomile tea throughout, since the lint asks for the thing and not the family, and chamomile is the tea tasters most often mean.

The name from the russet colour of the ripe berries (the Codex's own bank; Inter Rhône gives a reddish golden colour when ripe) was written and then left out of the shown text, so that no two grapes of the chunk open on the colour of a skin.

The California vines sold as Roussanne and shown by DNA to be Viognier stand on Capstone California, the study programme of the state's Wine Institute, and on a Wine Spectator report of 2000; no person or house is named. The year of the test is given only as the 1990s.
Savoie is placed on the cool rung although the Codex notes Roussanne needs warm sites there to ripen. No Creole dish is given: none of the seven suits better than the dishes listed.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.

The worlds reading of 11 November 2026 moved Roussanne to home and abroad, with plan.json, as this report foresaw: the Codex Central Coast and Swartland records hold New World Roussanne as a part of Rhône style blends, and the varietal bottles are too few to set a second style beside the Rhône and Savoie. The worlds question became a blind glass from Saint-Joseph.

checked.verdict: Sound after seven fixes. The California vines sold as Roussanne and found to be Viognier, Bergeron and Chignin-Bergeron, the white grapes Châteauneuf-du-Pape permits (Marsanne and Viognier not among them), honeysuckle, iris and hawthorn among the notes, and varietal Roussanne from Washington were confirmed.
changed: questions[2]: the stem asked which grape is not permitted in a white Châteauneuf-du-Pape, a negative question of the kind the brief refuses. It now asks which pair the appellation may use, with four pairs of grapes and one key, Roussanne and Grenache Blanc.

worlds.contrast.call: honey is taken off the New World side. The same entry gives Savoie apricot and honey in its Old World glass, its label row and its first card, so honey could not part the worlds; baked pear and a warmer, broader finish do.
cards[1].back: the same change, to agree with the call.

questions[0].exp: honey no longer points to the New World there either; the explanation leans on the baked pear, the oily feel and the warm, broad finish, and says Chignin-Bergeron can show honey too.

worlds.contrast.why: the rules of the Rhône name places and favour blends now reads its labels name places and its growers favour blends. No rule asks for a blend: Hermitage may be all Roussanne, and one cru of Savoie must be.
glass.notes: the herbal group (chamomile tea, white tea) is struck and chamomile tea joins the floral notes. White tea stood in no source read; sources say a flowery herbal tea.
profile.other: white tea gives way to hawthorn blossom, which the notes already hold.
open: The plan gives the side by side and the author doubted it. It stands: varietal bottles from Paso Robles and from Washington are a style a guest meets, though the Swartland uses the grape in blends, as the Codex says.

INTRO_GRAPES gives the wines of Roussanne as Hermitage, Châteauneuf-du-Pape blanc (with Marsanne). Marsanne is not on the list Châteauneuf-du-Pape permits; the author is right and the entry is kept right.
Chamomile stands for the herbal tea of the reference works; it is the author's choice of the thing for the family, and no source read names chamomile itself.
The Régionale bank says Roussanne ripens late and the Rhône body is quoted as early to mid; the entry states neither.
